body:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Aurora DevTools — beta check-in: shadow traffic quality metrics (week 2)
Date/Time: 2026-02-05 10:03 AM PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Marissa Cole, Dylan Brooks, Jonas Weber, Allison Grant
Aurora DevTools: Lena Ortiz, Sanjay Patel, Rebecca Cho, Omar Nasser

Summary (auto-generated)
- Reviewed first 10 days of shadow traffic results comparing control vs candidate model variant on Aurora Dedicated.
- Discussed dashboard usability feedback: confidence intervals, sample size visibility, and filtering/segmentation.
- Agreed to expand sampling on a single route with guardrails and to investigate scoring lag incident.

Topics
1) Early results: quality deltas vs baseline
2) Scoring lag + pipeline health
3) Dashboard feedback: segmentation, exports, and examples
4) Next steps: expand sampling safely + rubric/versioning

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to investigate scoring lag spike on 02/03.
- Redwood to refine format adherence metric and reduce false positives.
- Aurora to share examples and expand sampling to 2% on one route.

Questions
- Can we segment by prompt template version without blowing up cardinality?
- How does fail-open work when shadow target is erroring or slow?
- What’s the retention window for prompts/responses in Dedicated?

Transcript

[00:00] Marissa Cole: Hey everyone. Thanks for joining. This is the week two beta check-in on the shadow quality metrics. Goal today is look at what you’re seeing in the dashboard, what feels off, and then decide if we can safely turn the sampling up on at least one route.

[00:18] Rebecca Cho: Sounds good.

[00:19] Lena Ortiz: Yep.

[00:21] Marissa Cole: Quick intros for the recording—Marissa, product for Console and rollouts. Dylan’s here from Console eng. Jonas is our evals/scoring lead. Allison from observability/alerting.

[00:34] Omar Nasser: Omar SRE on our side.

[00:36] Sanjay Patel: Sanjay ML eng.

[00:38] Rebecca Cho: Rebecca PM.

[00:42] Marissa Cole: Great. So we pulled the latest snapshot through yesterday end of day. You’ve been running at, I think, 0.5% sampling on /chat/support and 0.2% on /chat/triage—does that match?

[00:56] Lena Ortiz: That’s what we configured, yep. We kept it low because we were worried about the extra spend and any weirdness with quotas.

[01:05] Allison Grant: Makes sense. And just to restate: the user response is always control. Shadow is mirrored with a tight timeout. If anything goes sideways we drop shadow and you still serve.

[01:16] Omar Nasser: Right, we did see some shadow errors but user latency didn’t move, which is good.

[01:22] Marissa Cole: Let’s start with quality. Jonas, can you summarize the deltas we’re showing?

[01:28] Jonas Weber: Yeah. So control is your current pinned model version, and shadow is the candidate variant you named “candidate-q4-kv2” in the experiment. Over the last 7 days, the headline metrics: refusal rate basically flat, like +0.1 percentage points, within noise. Safety heuristic triggers are also flat.

[01:47] Jonas Weber: The notable one is format adherence. We’re showing a -2.4% delta in “valid structured output” for the candidate, with a 95% CI that doesn’t cross zero for that window.

[02:00] Sanjay Patel: That’s the one that surprised us because qualitatively, when we clicked examples, most looked fine. It’s like, the model returns JSON but then it adds a sentence after.

[02:09] Jonas Weber: Yep. That’s exactly what I saw in a couple. The current heuristic is strict: it wants the response to parse cleanly as JSON if you asked for JSON. If there’s trailing commentary it flags it.

[02:22] Rebecca Cho: But in our app we strip everything after the last brace. So the customer outcome is still okay.

[02:27] Dylan Brooks: That’s super useful. The metric as shipped is intentionally conservative, but we probably need a knob or a more nuanced “parseable JSON present” vs “strict only JSON.”

[02:39] Marissa Cole: This is good feedback. For beta we’re trying to catch real regressions, not annoy you with false positives.

[02:46] Sanjay Patel: Also we had a prompt template update mid-week, and I couldn’t tell if the dashboard is mixing those or not.

[02:53] Allison Grant: Right now the default breakdown is by route and model variant, plus coarse region. We intentionally don’t break down by prompt ID because cardinality. But we can do prompt template version if you have a small set.

[03:08] Lena Ortiz: We have like… three templates in production for that route, and version numbers are stable. That should be safe.

[03:15] Allison Grant: Okay, that’s doable. We can add “prompt_template_version” as an allowlisted dimension for your tenant if it stays low-cardinality.

[03:24] Marissa Cole: Let’s park that as a next step. On the other metrics: instruction following score looked slightly improved, right?

[03:31] Jonas Weber: Yeah. The model-graded “instruction following rubric” is +0.06 on a 0–1 scale. It’s modest but consistent. The confidence interval is narrow-ish given your sample size, but I want to be careful because the grader model can drift. We’ve pinned rubric version v0.3 for your experiment.

[03:51] Sanjay Patel: Can you explain rubric version pinning again? Our leadership asked if we can compare week one to week three if the rubric changes.

[03:58] Jonas Weber: Sure. Each experiment run stores “rubric_version.” If we update to v0.4 later, you can still keep running v0.3 for continuity. If you change rubric versions, we’ll show a banner that comparisons across runs are not apples-to-apples.

[04:17] Rebecca Cho: That’s good. We probably want continuity for now.

[04:20] Marissa Cole: Let’s shift to the dashboard feedback. Dylan, you had notes from the thread you sent.

[04:27] Dylan Brooks: Yeah. We saw three main things you all mentioned in the comments: one, the sample size “N” isn’t visible enough. Two, the confidence intervals are there but kind of buried in the chart toggles. And three, the examples view is helpful but you want quicker export or share links.

[04:45] Lena Ortiz: Exactly. Our exec sees “-2.4% format adherence” and panics, but they don’t see it’s based on like 1,800 samples.

[04:54] Dylan Brooks: Totally. We can add N in the main header next to the metric, with control and shadow counts. And we can make CI the default band on charts.

[05:05] Omar Nasser: Also, the time window selection is confusing. It defaults to last 24 hours, but with low sampling that’s noisy.

[05:12] Allison Grant: That’s a good point. We can add a “recommended minimum window” hint based on observed sample rate. Like if you’re at 0.2%, last 24 hours might be 80 samples, which is meaningless.

[05:25] Marissa Cole: Nice. Jonas, anything else on interpretation pitfalls?

[05:29] Jonas Weber: Just that format adherence is sometimes correlated with verbosity. Candidate might be more chatty. That’s not always worse, but if your downstream parser is strict, it matters. So we want to separate “structural compliance” from “verbosity drift.”

[05:46] Sanjay Patel: That’s exactly it. Our downstream is not strict, but our QA harness is strict. So we need to know both.

[06:00] Marissa Cole: Great. So early results are: no safety regressions, slight instruction-following improvement, and a format adherence warning that may be false-positive for your app.

[06:12] Marissa Cole: Next, scoring lag. Omar, you mentioned you saw backlog.

[06:16] Omar Nasser: Yeah, on Feb 3rd afternoon, the “scoring freshness” widget showed 15, 18 minutes. I think it cleared later, but we weren’t sure if we should dial sampling down.

[06:28] Allison Grant: I saw that too. The SLO for the scoring pipeline in beta is <10 minutes p95 lag. When it goes above, we don’t page you—only page Redwood oncall—but the dashboard should show it clearly.

[06:43] Lena Ortiz: It did show it, but we didn’t know the right action.

[06:46] Marissa Cole: We should probably add guidance: if lag is high, you can keep it on, but don’t make decisions on the last hour. The system is “fail-open” for serving, but quality data will be delayed.

[06:59] Allison Grant: Also the circuit breaker: if lag is extreme, or ingestion is backpressured, we start dropping shadow events, so your effective sample rate goes down.

[07:11] Sanjay Patel: Is there a way to tell if the sample rate is being reduced by the system vs our config?

[07:16] Allison Grant: Yes, there’s a “delivered shadow rate” metric vs “configured sample rate.” It’s in the experiment diagnostics panel. I can send a screenshot after.

[07:27] Marissa Cole: Great. So action item: Allison will investigate that spike and tell you root cause.

[07:34] Allison Grant: Yep.

[07:36] Marissa Cole: Now, next steps on expanding sampling. You’re currently low. Would you be comfortable increasing to 2% on /chat/support, but only during off-peak?

[07:49] Lena Ortiz: Possibly. Our traffic is high. 2% is still a lot of tokens.

[07:55] Sanjay Patel: The main constraint is cost. We don’t want to pay for candidate tokens for weeks.

[08:01] Marissa Cole: Understood. For beta, we can keep scoring limited to the default bundle and a short retention window, and we can cap daily shadow tokens. There’s also a mode where we mirror requests but only score a subset of them.

[08:17] Sanjay Patel: That might be the sweet spot. Mirror 2%, score maybe 25% of those.

[08:23] Jonas Weber: Yep. The reason is statistical power: you need enough samples to detect a ~1–2% change. But you don’t necessarily need to grade every single one. We can do stratified scoring.

[08:35] Omar Nasser: Does that change the CI math? Like, you’re sampling twice.

[08:39] Jonas Weber: Good question. We account for it in the effective N for scored metrics. For non-scored metrics like shadow error rate and latency, those use the mirrored set.

[08:52] Rebecca Cho: And what about user privacy? We still have some concerns about prompts in logs.

[08:57] Marissa Cole: We should cover that. This is Dedicated, so by default we store redacted artifacts with short retention. Allison or Jonas, can you say what’s on by default?

[09:07] Allison Grant: Default in Dedicated beta: prompts and outputs are truncated to a max length, and we hash stable identifiers. We drop request headers by default, except for an allowlist. Retention is 7 days for raw artifacts, longer for aggregates. You can shorten it.

[09:25] Lena Ortiz: Good. We’ll want to confirm which headers are mirrored. We have some customer identifiers we can’t let through.

[09:31] Dylan Brooks: That’s part of the shadow policy config—what metadata gets passed. Right now you’re in “safe mode,” meaning we only forward minimal context. If you want more, it’s explicit.

[09:44] Sanjay Patel: Okay.

[09:45] Marissa Cole: So proposal: expand sampling on one route to 2% for mirroring, score 25% of mirrored, run it for 5 days, segment by prompt template version, and then review.

[10:01] Rebecca Cho: Works for me.

[10:02] Lena Ortiz: Off-peak only though.

[10:04] Marissa Cole: We don’t have a time-of-day scheduler in policy yet, but we can do it operationally—flip it at, say, 7 PM to 7 AM PT. Or we can set a daily token cap.

[10:17] Omar Nasser: Token cap is better. We can’t rely on manual flips.

[10:21] Allison Grant: We can set a hard cap and it will stop shadowing when it’s hit, fail-open.

[10:28] Sanjay Patel: Great.

[10:31] Marissa Cole: Cool. Dashboard feedback—what else did you want to see?

[10:35] Lena Ortiz: Two things. One, “example drilldown” needs quicker navigation. Like next/prev, and show control vs shadow side-by-side with highlighting.

[10:44] Dylan Brooks: Got it. We have side-by-side already but highlighting is coming.

[10:49] Lena Ortiz: Second, export. We want to pull a CSV of the aggregates for our weekly exec review.

[10:56] Dylan Brooks: There’s an API endpoint in beta but it’s not documented well. We can give you a curl snippet and then the SDK support is coming.

[11:07] Rebecca Cho: That’s fine.

[11:08] Sanjay Patel: Also, I noticed the chart can be “green” even when the CI overlaps. We’d rather have a neutral state.

[11:15] Dylan Brooks: Yeah, right now it labels based on point estimate only. We can change it to: regression only if CI is entirely below zero past threshold; improvement only if entirely above; otherwise neutral.

[11:31] Marissa Cole: That lines up with the observability standard we want.

[11:34] Allison Grant: +1.

[11:36] Marissa Cole: One more question: do you want quality signals to trigger rollback automation eventually? Or advisory only for now.

[11:45] Rebecca Cho: Advisory for now. We’re not ready to auto-rollback based on a rubric that might be wrong.

[11:52] Omar Nasser: Agreed. We can use it as a gate in our process, but not automated.

[11:58] Marissa Cole: Great. That’s also our default at launch.

[12:03] Jonas Weber: If we do get confidence, we can set thresholds later, but we want to earn trust first.

[12:12] Marissa Cole: Okay. Let’s check on the “format adherence” false positives. Sanjay, you said your app strips trailing text. Could you share a handful of cases where we flagged failure but your parser accepted it?

[12:23] Sanjay Patel: Yes. I’ll send like 10 examples. Some are fenced JSON with backticks. Some are JSON plus a sentence.

[12:31] Jonas Weber: Perfect. We can update the heuristic to accept fenced JSON and ignore trailing whitespace/commentary, but we need to be careful not to let real schema breaks through.

[12:44] Lena Ortiz: Another angle: we sometimes request “JSON with keys x,y,z” but we don’t care about order. The metric shouldn’t fail for ordering.

[12:52] Jonas Weber: It doesn’t care about order today, but it does care about missing keys.

[12:56] Sanjay Patel: Cool.

[13:00] Marissa Cole: I’m going to jump a bit—any latency or overhead concerns you saw?

[13:05] Omar Nasser: User path latency didn’t change. For shadow, the shadow latency is higher, but it doesn’t matter. However, we did see some extra CPU on the routing layer.

[13:15] Allison Grant: That’s expected but should be within the guardrails. We can share the overhead dashboard. The data plane mirror is async; it’s designed not to block.

[13:28] Lena Ortiz: We’re fine as long as it doesn’t increase our tail lat for actual users.

[13:33] Marissa Cole: Exactly.

[13:36] Dylan Brooks: One more thing: streaming requests. Are you using streaming on these routes?

[13:41] Sanjay Patel: Not on /chat/support. On /chat/triage, yes.

[13:45] Dylan Brooks: Streaming shadowing is supported but in a partial capture mode. It might affect scoring because we may truncate if it takes too long.

[13:55] Sanjay Patel: That’s okay. We can keep the expanded sampling on /chat/support which is non-streaming.

[14:01] Marissa Cole: Great.

[14:03] (crosstalk)

[14:04] Rebecca Cho: Sorry—one more dashboard thing. The “refusal rate” definition is unclear. It flagged a couple outputs that were basically “I can’t access your internal ticketing system.” That’s not a safety refusal, that’s capability.

[14:18] Jonas Weber: Yeah, that’s a classic. The heuristic currently looks for refusal-like phrases. We should probably split “policy refusal” vs “capability limitation.”

[14:29] Marissa Cole: That’s good product feedback. For v1 we may keep it simple but we can at least improve labeling.

[14:38] Allison Grant: And it helps with alerting. You don’t want to page people because the model said “I can’t browse.”

[14:45] Omar Nasser: Exactly.

[14:47] Marissa Cole: Okay, let’s recap decisions and next steps.

[15:00] Marissa Cole: 1) Expand sampling on /chat/support: configured mirror rate 2%, score 25% of mirrored; add daily token cap. Lena, you’ll coordinate on the header allowlist. 2) Allison investigates Feb 3 scoring lag spike. 3) Jonas proposes a tweak to format adherence heuristic, based on your examples. 4) Dylan updates UI: surface N and CI more clearly, and neutral state when CI overlaps. 5) We enable segmentation by prompt_template_version if it stays at ~3 values.

[15:35] Lena Ortiz: Yep.

[15:36] Sanjay Patel: Works.

[15:37] Rebecca Cho: Great.

[15:39] Marissa Cole: Any other questions before we end?

[15:42] Omar Nasser: Just one. If shadow target starts erroring, do you keep sending to it and waste resources?

[15:49] Allison Grant: No. There’s a circuit breaker. If error rate crosses threshold or timeouts spike, we back off and stop mirroring to that target for a cooldown window. Control path is unaffected.

[16:02] Omar Nasser: Perfect.

[16:03] Sanjay Patel: And we can see that in diagnostics?

[16:06] Allison Grant: Yes—“shadow delivered rate” drops and we show a banner like “shadow target degraded, fail-open engaged.”

[16:15] Sanjay Patel: Great.

[16:17] Marissa Cole: Cool. We’ll send a follow-up email with the updated plan and the links to the dashboard sections. Thanks everyone.

[16:25] (meeting ends / recording stops)

Note: Transcript may contain inaccuracies due to automated speech recognition.
